evidence.label: The Margulis–Platonov conjecture over global function fields
The Margulis–Platonov conjecture over number fields

headline: Normal subgroups of these simple groups over any global field are claimed to come from finitely many local pieces.
scope: The groups are absolutely almost simple, simply connected algebraic groups over a number field or a global function field.
plain: Take a matrix group such as the 2 × 2 matrices of determinant 1 with fraction entries. A normal subgroup is a part of it that conjugation never moves outside itself. The Margulis–Platonov conjecture says such parts come only from finitely many compact local groups. Two papers claim to prove it: one over number fields, one over function fields, including characteristic two. Many cases were already known; these papers claim the remaining ones.
doesNot: This does not settle Serre's congruence subgroup conjecture in general, only a positive-density case that follows from it.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: G. A. Margulis, who formulated the description by anisotropic local factors
scorecard.significanceWhy: It claims the last open types of a long-standing conjecture on normal subgroups of arithmetic groups.

explanation:
Take the 2 × 2 matrices with fraction entries and determinant 1. The matrix with rows (2, 1) and (1, 1) is one. Its determinant is 2 × 1 − 1 × 1 = 1. Together these matrices form a group called SL₂ over the rationals. A normal subgroup is a part that stays inside itself when you conjugate by any member. The center here is just the identity and its negative. For this group, any normal subgroup bigger than the center is the whole group.

Not every such group is that rigid. Now take quaternions a + bi + cj + dk with fraction coefficients. Here i, j and k are three square roots of −1 with ij = k. Keep those with a² + b² + c² + d² = 1. One example is 3/5 + 4/5 i, since 9/25 + 16/25 = 1. These form a group too, but it can have many normal subgroups. The reason is local. Viewed with 2-adic numbers (a way of measuring numbers by divisibility by 2), this group becomes compact (closed and bounded). Compact local groups have many open normal subgroups, and these pull back to the rational group.

The Margulis–Platonov conjecture says that is the only source. Take a group G of the kind studied, called absolutely almost simple and simply connected. Collect the finitely many places where G becomes anisotropic, so its local group is compact[1]. Then every normal subgroup not inside the center comes from an open normal subgroup of the product of those compact groups[2]. When there are no such places, the only option is the whole group[3]. The normal subgroups are abstract: no extra condition is put on them[4].

The conjecture grew from a question of Kneser on quaternions and a proposal of Platonov. Margulis formulated it in 1979[5]. Many cases followed. Groups with no compact local places were handled through the Kneser–Tits theorem[6]. Chernousov treated many anisotropic groups[7]. For inner type A, built from division algebras, Segev and Segev–Seitz completed the case[8]. Rapinchuk, Segev and Seitz later proved it over all global fields for that type[13]. The open cases were certain outer type A, triality D₄ and E₆ groups over number fields[9].

The number-field paper claims to settle those remaining cases[2,9]. The function-field paper claims the conjecture over every global function field, a field built from polynomials over a finite field[10]. That includes characteristic two. There, earlier results had already reduced the problem to special unitary groups of outer type A[11].

The hard step is a finite obstruction. Known tools show a normal subgroup has finite index. They also show its closure matches the local picture. What remains is a finite gap between the abstract subgroup and that closure[12]. For the special unitary groups, the paper rules out a finite simple group as the quotient. It colors each rational element by its image, then argues that a translation-invariant random coloring leads to a contradiction.

The number-field paper also gives a consequence for the congruence subgroup property. Feeding the theorem into a 2026 theorem of Rapinchuk gives that property when the set S of places has positive density[14]. It does not address Serre’s conjecture for finite S[15].

How sure is this? No Lean formalization is listed for these papers in the openai/math release. So no computer proof checker has checked them. The proofs rely on deep results, including the classification of finite simple groups. No specialist review has been published.
hypeCheck: Major only if both papers hold. No Lean formalization is listed and no specialist review is published. Many cases were proved by others; these papers claim the remaining ones.

glossary.meaning: A part of a group that conjugation by any member keeps inside itself.
The members of a group that commute with every member.
For these groups, having a compact local group, with no unipotent elements to move things far.
Closed and bounded, so that every sequence has a limit point inside.
A number system that measures size by divisibility by a prime p.
A number field, or a field of rational functions over a finite field and its finite extensions.
The property that every finite-index normal subgroup contains a subgroup defined by congruences.
